nameStory: The red-tailed hawk gets its name from its most distinctive feature – that gorgeous brick-red tail that catches the light as it soars overhead. When you see one circling high above a field, that rusty-red tail is often your first clue to its identity, like a built-in name tag flashing in the sky.
description: The red-tailed hawk is one of New England's most common and impressive birds of prey, built like a feathered linebacker with broad wings perfect for soaring. These stocky raptors measure about 18-26 inches long with wingspans that can stretch nearly 5 feet across – big enough to cast a noticeable shadow when they pass overhead. Females are noticeably larger than males, sometimes weighing nearly twice as much, which is typical for most hawks and eagles.

idTips.label: Brick-red tail
idTips.description: Adults sport a distinctive rusty-red tail that glows like a traffic light when backlit by the sun – you'll often spot this color from quite a distance as they soar

idTips.label: Broad wings and stocky build
idTips.description: Much bulkier than other hawks with wide, rounded wings that they hold in a slight upward angle while soaring – think of a flying coffee table compared to the narrow-winged sharp-shinned hawk

idTips.label: Characteristic call
idTips.description: Their piercing 'keeee-ahhhh' scream carries for miles – that classic hawk cry you hear in movies is usually a red-tailed hawk, with a hoarse, descending whistle that sounds like steam escaping

idTips.label: Soaring behavior
idTips.description: Often seen riding thermals high overhead with wings spread wide and barely moving, circling slowly like they're riding an invisible elevator in the sky

idTips.label: Perching posture
idTips.description: Sits very upright on fence posts, dead trees, and utility poles with a proud, alert stance – like a feathered sentinel watching over their territory

idTips.label: Dark belly band
idTips.description: Many adults show a distinctive dark band across their pale belly when viewed from below, though this varies – some are heavily streaked while others are nearly white underneath

habitat: Red-tailed hawks are habitat generalists that thrive almost anywhere with a mix of open hunting grounds and tall perches – from suburban neighborhoods with big trees to farmland, forest edges, and highway corridors. You'll often spot them perched on utility poles along interstates or soaring over fields, pastures, and large lawns where they hunt for rodents. They avoid dense, unbroken forests but love forest edges, parks, and even urban areas as long as there are tall trees for nesting and open spaces for hunting.

seasonality.spring: Breeding season brings dramatic aerial courtship displays with pairs diving and calling together, plus the construction of large stick nests high in trees. Young birds from the previous year disperse to find their own territories during this time.
seasonality.summer: Adults are busy raising their 1-3 chicks, making frequent hunting trips and bringing prey back to the nest. You might hear the constant begging calls of hungry young hawks echoing from tall trees.
seasonality.fall: Migration season brings northern red-tails through New England, though many are year-round residents. Juvenile birds show brown, banded tails instead of red – they won't get their signature red tail until their second year.
seasonality.winter: Many red-tails remain active year-round in New England, often more visible as they perch prominently in bare trees. Some northern birds move south, while others arrive from even farther north to spend winter here.

funFact: Red-tailed hawks are such skilled and common hunters that the majority of hawks used in falconry across the United States are red-tails – they're basically the golden retrievers of the raptor world, smart enough to train but wild enough to be impressive hunting partners.
confusionNotes: Young red-tailed hawks lack the red tail and are often confused with red-shouldered hawks, but red-tails are bulkier with broader wings and that distinctive dark belly band. Remember: if it's soaring high with broad wings and looks chunky, it's probably a red-tail, while red-shouldered hawks prefer flying low through forests and have a more slender build.
contextualKnowledge: Red-tailed hawks are one of three species sometimes called 'chickenhawks' in folklore, though they rarely bother chickens and actually help farmers by controlling rodent populations. Their feathers and other parts are considered sacred by many Native American tribes, and they're protected under federal law – it's illegal to possess their feathers without special permits.
compareHints: Among New England's buteo hawks, red-tails are the largest and bulkiest, while red-shouldered hawks are more slender with distinctive reddish shoulder patches and prefer wooded areas. Broad-winged hawks are much smaller and chunkier, and most migrate south for winter, unlike the year-round red-tails. The rare rough-legged hawks that visit in winter have feathered legs all the way to their toes and hover more frequently while hunting.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among buteo hawks in New England, red-shouldered hawks are the forest specialists with the most distinctive barring pattern.
Compared to its buteo relatives, the broad-winged hawk is the most forest-dependent and migratory.
Unlike the year-round resident Red-tailed and Red-shouldered Hawks, Rough-legged Hawks are strictly winter visitors from the Arctic.
Compared to our common Red-tailed and Red-shouldered Hawks, Swainson's Hawks have longer, more pointed wings and are built more for long-distance soaring.
Ferruginous hawks absolutely dwarf their buteo relatives – they're significantly larger than red-tailed hawks with much broader wings and a more massive build.
